title: From the 1970s to the Present
bigQuestion: Since 1969 Americans have lived through scandals, shocks, booms and a pandemic. How do we tell which of these events changed the country, and how can we judge a past we are still living in?

story.title: Grant Park, Election Night
story.kicker: On a mild November night in 2008, more than two hundred thousand people filled a Chicago park to watch a senator from Illinois become president.
paragraphs: By early evening on November 4, 2008, the lawns of Grant Park along Michigan Avenue were full. People had lined up since the afternoon. Some held tickets; many more stood outside the fences, watching giant screens. The weather was unseasonably warm for Chicago in November, and the crowd, by most estimates, grew past two hundred thousand. Office windows in the Loop glowed above them. Fifty-year-olds who remembered the riots of 1968 stood next to college students who had knocked on doors in Iowa that January.

The man they were waiting for had come to Chicago in 1985, at twenty-four, to work as a community organizer with churches on the Far South Side, in Roseland and the Altgeld Gardens housing project, neighborhoods hollowed out when the steel mills closed. He left for Harvard Law School, came back, married a lawyer from South Shore named Michelle Robinson, taught constitutional law at the University of Chicago and won a state senate seat from Hyde Park in 1996. In 2004 a speech at the Democratic convention made him famous, and Illinois sent him to the United States Senate. In February 2007 he announced his run for president on the steps of the Old State Capitol in Springfield, where Lincoln had warned in 1858 that a house divided could not stand.

At ten o'clock Central time, when the polls closed on the West Coast, the television networks called the election for Barack Obama. The park erupted. Cameras found Jesse Jackson, who had stood beside Martin Luther King Jr. in Memphis in 1968, with tears running down his face. Around eleven the new president-elect walked out with his family. He told the crowd, in words this book can only paraphrase, that anyone who still doubted that America was a place where all things were possible had received their answer that night. He spoke of a voter in Atlanta, Ann Nixon Cooper, who was one hundred six years old and had been born when neither women nor Black Americans could cast a ballot.

The same park held other memories and other facts. Forty years earlier, police and antiwar protesters had fought in Grant Park during the 1968 Democratic convention. Seven weeks before election night, the investment bank Lehman Brothers had collapsed, and the country was sliding into the deepest downturn since the 1930s. The United States was fighting two wars. Nearly sixty million Americans had voted for the other candidate, John McCain. Many of the people cheering in the park would lose a job or a house in the year ahead.

This chapter runs from 1969 to the present. It is the hardest kind of history to write, because the people who lived it are still arguing about what it meant, and because you are one of them. Watergate, the oil shocks, the Reagan years, the end of the Cold War, the internet, September 11, the crash of 2008, the Obama presidency, polarization and a pandemic: each is a case for testing how historians decide what mattered. Grant Park in 2008 is where the story turns, and where the questions begin.
story.think: The same park saw police clubbing protesters in 1968 and a celebration in 2008. What does the distance between those two nights tell you, and what does it leave out?

lessons.title: Watergate
lessons.mainIdea: Watergate began as a burglary and ended a presidency because tape recordings proved the president had obstructed justice, and because courts, Congress and the press each did their job.
reading: At about two in the morning on June 17, 1972, a security guard named Frank Wills noticed tape holding a door latch open at the *Watergate* office complex in Washington, D.C. He removed it. When he came back, the tape was there again, so he called the police. Officers arrested five men inside the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee carrying cameras, bugging equipment and cash. One of them, James McCord, worked for the Committee to Re-elect the President, Richard Nixon's campaign. The White House called it a third-rate burglary. That November Nixon won forty-nine states. The break-in itself was a small crime. What destroyed Nixon was the *cover-up*: the effort to hide who had ordered it and paid for it.

Two young reporters at the Washington Post, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, followed the money from the burglars back to the campaign, helped by a secret source inside the FBI whom they called Deep Throat. In 1973 the Senate opened televised hearings led by Sam Ervin of North Carolina. Nixon's former lawyer, John Dean, testified that the president had joined the cover-up. Then, in July, an aide named Alexander Butterfield revealed that Nixon secretly recorded his Oval Office conversations. The *special prosecutor*, Archibald Cox, demanded the tapes. On October 20, 1973, Nixon ordered him fired. The attorney general and his deputy resigned rather than do it, in what the press called the Saturday Night Massacre.

On July 24, 1974, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in United States v. Nixon that a president's *executive privilege*, his right to keep advice confidential, was real but not absolute, and that he had to hand over the tapes. Days later the House Judiciary Committee, with votes from both parties, approved articles of *impeachment* for obstruction of justice, abuse of power and contempt of Congress. On August 5 the White House released a tape from June 23, 1972, on which Nixon told aides to have the CIA block the FBI's investigation. Republican senators told him he would be convicted. Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, the only president ever to do so. Gerald Ford took office and, a month later, pardoned him.

How do we know all this? The tapes sit in the National Archives, and anyone can listen to them online. The hearings were broadcast; the court opinion is public; dozens of officials were convicted and their trial records survive. Historians also point out that the system worked only because individuals chose to act: a night guard, two reporters, a judge named John Sirica who pressed the burglars to talk, senators of both parties, and a Court that included justices Nixon himself had appointed. Remove any one, and the story might have ended differently.

words.d: the 1972 break-in at Democratic headquarters and the cover-up that forced President Nixon to resign in 1974
an effort to hide a crime or wrongdoing, which is often a crime itself
a lawyer appointed from outside the normal chain of command to investigate high officials
a president's claim to keep advice and conversations confidential; limited by the courts in 1974
the House's formal charge against an official, followed by a Senate trial that can remove them

look.title: The Court Rules on the Tapes
look.text: In a paraphrase of its unanimous opinion, the Court said that a president does have a legitimate interest in keeping his conversations private, and that courts must respect it. But a general claim of confidentiality, with no military or diplomatic secret involved, cannot outweigh the need for evidence in a criminal trial. The demand for every person's evidence applies to the president too.
look.cite: Supreme Court, United States v. Nixon, July 24, 1974 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Three of the eight justices who ruled against Nixon had been appointed by him. Why does that fact matter for how much weight we give the decision?

check.q: According to the lesson, what actually forced Nixon from office?
choices: The cover-up, proven by his own tape recordings
The burglary at the Watergate complex itself
Losing the 1972 election
A vote of the full Senate to remove him
check.why: The break-in was minor; the June 23 tape proved Nixon had ordered the FBI investigation blocked, and he resigned before a Senate trial.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in United States v. Nixon?
choices: Presidents can never keep any conversation secret
Executive privilege exists but could not block evidence needed in a criminal case
The tapes belonged to Nixon personally
Congress could not impeach a sitting president
check.why: The Court recognized the privilege but ruled it was not absolute, and ordered the tapes turned over.

check.q: Why does the lesson stress the night guard, the reporters and the judge?
choices: They were the only people who broke the law
They were all appointed by Nixon
The outcome depended on individual choices, not just on the system's design
They wrote the Constitution's impeachment clause
check.why: The lesson argues that the checks worked because specific people chose to act at each step.

lessons.title: Trust After Watergate
lessons.mainIdea: Vietnam, Watergate and revelations about the CIA and FBI drove public trust in government down sharply, and Congress answered with laws that limit presidents and open records.
reading: Since 1958 pollsters have asked Americans whether they trust the government in Washington to do what is right most of the time. In 1964 about three in four said yes. By 1974 barely one in three did. Watergate was only part of the reason. In 1971 the New York Times published the Pentagon Papers, a secret Defense Department history leaked by an analyst named Daniel Ellsberg, which showed that presidents of both parties had misled the public about Vietnam. Nixon's response was to create a secret unit, nicknamed the Plumbers, that broke into Ellsberg's psychiatrist's office. The same men later broke into the Watergate. Reporters called the gap between what officials said and what was true the *credibility gap*.

Congress moved to rein in the presidency. The *War Powers Resolution* of November 1973, passed over Nixon's veto, requires a president to notify Congress within forty-eight hours of sending troops into combat and to withdraw them within sixty days unless Congress approves. A 1974 budget law created the Congressional Budget Office so lawmakers no longer depended on the White House for numbers. New campaign finance rules set limits on contributions and created the Federal Election Commission. Amendments to the *Freedom of Information Act*, passed over Ford's veto in 1974, made it far easier for citizens and reporters to demand government files. The Twenty-sixth Amendment, ratified in 1971, had already lowered the voting age to eighteen.

In 1975 a Senate committee led by Frank Church of Idaho investigated the intelligence agencies. The *Church Committee* found that the CIA had plotted to assassinate foreign leaders, opened Americans' mail and tested drugs on people without consent, and that the FBI's COINTELPRO program had spied on and tried to break up civil rights groups, including the effort against Martin Luther King Jr. described in the last chapter. The result was permanent intelligence oversight committees in both houses and, in 1978, a special court that must approve spying on people inside the United States.

Gerald Ford, the only president never elected to either the presidency or the vice presidency, paid for the pardon at the polls. In 1976 voters chose Jimmy Carter, a Georgia peanut farmer and former governor who promised he would never lie to them. Carter brokered the Camp David peace accords between Egypt and Israel in 1978, but inflation and a hostage crisis in Iran wore down his presidency. Trust never returned to 1960s levels. It spiked briefly after September 11, 2001, then fell to about one in five by the 2010s. Some argue that healthy suspicion is what the framers intended. Others point out that low trust makes it harder to govern in an emergency. Both sides are reading the same numbers.

words.d: the distance between what officials said and what was true, a phrase from the Vietnam years
the 1973 law requiring presidents to report troop deployments to Congress and withdraw within sixty days without approval
a law, strengthened in 1974, that lets anyone request government records
the 1975 Senate investigation that exposed abuses by the CIA and FBI and led to permanent oversight

look.title: Trust in the Federal Government
look.unit: % trusting Washington most of the time
look.cite: American National Election Studies and Pew Research Center, rounded
look.prompt: Trust fell before Watergate ended and jumped after September 11. What besides scandal seems to move this number, and what would you want to know before trusting it?

check.q: What did the Pentagon Papers reveal?
choices: That Nixon had ordered the Watergate break-in
That the CIA had plotted against foreign leaders
That the Soviets had bugged the Pentagon
That leaders of both parties had misled the public about Vietnam
check.why: The leaked Defense Department history showed a pattern of official statements that did not match the facts.

check.q: What does the War Powers Resolution require?
choices: Presidents must notify Congress within forty-eight hours of sending troops and withdraw within sixty days without approval
Congress must declare war before any troops move
The president must get United Nations approval for combat
The Senate must approve every general
check.why: The 1973 law, passed over Nixon's veto, set reporting and time limits on presidential use of force.

check.q: Why did the Church Committee lead to permanent oversight committees?
choices: The CIA asked for more funding
It found the CIA and FBI had acted illegally against Americans and foreign leaders without anyone checking them
It discovered the Watergate tapes
It proved the agencies had done nothing wrong
check.why: The committee's findings about assassination plots and COINTELPRO convinced Congress that spy agencies needed watching.

lessons.title: Oil Shocks and Stagflation
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1970s two oil shocks and rising prices combined with high unemployment into stagflation, a problem the old economic playbook could not solve, and the cure of the early 1980s was painful.
reading: In October 1973, during a war between Israel and its Arab neighbors, the Arab members of *OPEC*, the cartel of oil-exporting countries, cut off shipments to the United States for supporting Israel. The *embargo* lasted five months. The price of a barrel of crude oil roughly quadrupled, from about three dollars to about twelve. Gas stations ran dry. Some states allowed drivers to buy gas only on odd or even days, depending on their license plate. Congress set a national speed limit of fifty-five miles per hour to save fuel. For the first time since the Second World War, Americans discovered that a decision made overseas could empty their tank.

Economists had believed that inflation and unemployment moved in opposite directions: fight one and you got more of the other. The 1970s broke that rule. Prices rose about eleven percent in 1974 while unemployment climbed past eight percent the next year. The combination got a new name, *stagflation*, stagnation plus inflation. Oil was the reason it spread so fast, because oil is an input to almost everything: fertilizer, plastics, trucking, heating. Nixon had tried freezing wages and prices in 1971; Ford handed out buttons reading Whip Inflation Now. Neither worked, because once people expect prices to rise, they raise their own prices and wages first, and the expectation feeds itself.

A second shock came in 1979, when a revolution in Iran cut its oil exports and prices doubled again. That July, Carter gave a televised speech arguing that the country's real crisis was one of confidence, not just energy; critics called it the malaise speech. In August he appointed Paul Volcker to lead the *Federal Reserve*, and Volcker raised interest rates until borrowing nearly stopped. The prime lending rate passed twenty percent in 1980. The recession that followed pushed unemployment to almost eleven percent in late 1982, the worst since the Depression. Inflation fell to about three percent by 1983 and stayed low for decades.

The pain landed hardest on the industrial Midwest, soon called the *Rust Belt*. In March 1980 Wisconsin Steel on Chicago's Southeast Side shut its gates without warning, throwing roughly three thousand people out of work; many never received the pay they were owed. U.S. Steel's South Works, which had employed about twenty thousand at its peak, shrank through the 1980s and closed in 1992. Whether Volcker's cure was worth the cost is still argued. To judge it, compare the inflation of 1980 with what came after, then walk the empty lakefront where the mills stood.

words.d: the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, a group of oil producers that coordinates output and prices
a government or cartel's refusal to trade with a country, used as a weapon
high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, as in the 1970s
the nation's central bank, which sets interest rates to steer inflation and employment
the Midwestern and Northeastern industrial region that lost factories and jobs from the 1970s on

look.title: The Gas Line
look.text: It is a January morning in 1974. A line of cars stretches around the block from a station on Western Avenue. A sign says No Gas After 10 Gallons. A man in a Wisconsin Steel jacket has been waiting forty minutes with the engine off to save fuel. Your license plate ends in an odd number, and today is the fourteenth. The station owner posts a new price, twenty cents higher than last month.
look.prompt: Who in this scene is making decisions, who is only reacting, and how would you find out whether the shortage was caused overseas, in Washington, or at the station itself?

check.q: Why did the 1973 oil embargo affect prices for so many goods, not just gasoline?
choices: The government taxed all goods to pay for oil
Stores raised prices to punish OPEC
Oil is an input to fertilizer, plastics, trucking and heating, so its cost spreads everywhere
The embargo also stopped food imports
check.why: The lesson explains that oil feeds into nearly every product and every delivery.

check.q: What did stagflation prove wrong?
choices: The idea that oil prices could rise
That the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates
That presidents could freeze wages
The belief that inflation and unemployment always move in opposite directions
check.why: In the 1970s both rose together, breaking the expected trade-off.

check.q: How did Paul Volcker's Federal Reserve bring inflation down?
choices: By raising interest rates until borrowing nearly stopped, causing a deep recession
By printing more money
By reopening the steel mills
By lowering the speed limit
check.why: Rates above twenty percent choked off spending; inflation fell to about three percent by 1983 at the cost of nearly eleven percent unemployment.

lessons.title: Reagan and the Right
lessons.mainIdea: Ronald Reagan, born in Illinois, led a conservative movement that cut taxes, trimmed regulation, built up the military and reset the debate about the size of government.
reading: Ronald Reagan was born in 1911 above a store in Tampico, Illinois, and grew up in Dixon, where as a teenager he worked summers as a lifeguard on the Rock River. After Eureka College he called baseball games on radio in Iowa, became a Hollywood actor and, in the 1950s, toured General Electric plants giving speeches about free enterprise. A Democrat in his youth, he switched parties and in 1964 gave a televised speech for Barry Goldwater that made him a star of the new *conservatism*. He won the governorship of California in 1966. The movement he led drew on many streams: business owners tired of regulation, evangelical Christians alarmed by cultural change, and voters who felt the government had failed in Vietnam and in the economy.

One of those streams ran through Illinois. In 1972 Congress passed the *Equal Rights Amendment*, which would have written equality of the sexes into the Constitution, and thirty states ratified it within a year. Then Phyllis Schlafly of Alton, Illinois, organized a campaign called STOP ERA, arguing it would end protections for homemakers and send women into the draft. Illinois became the key battleground; its legislature voted the amendment down repeatedly, and the amendment fell three states short when its deadline passed in 1982. Schlafly showed that a grassroots movement on the right could beat one on the left, a lesson the conservative movement carried into 1980.

That year Reagan beat Carter in a landslide, asking voters whether they were better off than four years before. In 1981 Congress cut income tax rates by about a quarter over three years, with the top rate falling from seventy to fifty percent; a 1986 law lowered it to twenty-eight. The theory, called *supply-side economics*, held that lower taxes would spur so much growth that revenue would recover. Reagan cut domestic programs, raised military spending sharply and pushed *deregulation* of airlines, trucking and banking. When air traffic controllers struck illegally in August 1981, he fired the roughly eleven thousand who refused to return, a signal to unions everywhere. He won re-election in 1984 with forty-nine states.

The results were mixed and are still argued. After the 1982 recession, the economy grew strongly for the rest of the decade with low inflation. But revenue did not keep up with spending, and the national debt roughly tripled to about 2.9 trillion dollars by 1989, a *deficit* that shaped every later budget fight. Inequality widened and homelessness became visible in cities. The administration was slow to respond to the AIDS epidemic, first identified in 1981. In 1986 the Iran-Contra affair revealed that officials had secretly sold arms to Iran and used the money to fund rebels in Nicaragua against a ban by Congress. Historians who call this a Reagan Revolution point to taxes and the tone; skeptics note that Social Security, Medicare and federal spending as a share of the economy barely changed.

words.d: a political outlook favoring smaller government, lower taxes, traditional values and a strong military
a proposed constitutional amendment on sex equality that passed Congress in 1972 but fell short of ratification
the theory that cutting taxes will spur enough growth to raise revenue
removing government rules on an industry such as airlines or banking
the gap when government spends more in a year than it collects; deficits add to the national debt

look.title: A New President Defines the Problem
look.text: In a paraphrase of his first inaugural address, Reagan said the country faced an economic crisis of inflation, unemployment and debt, and that in this crisis government was not the solution to the problem but was itself the problem. He argued that the federal government had grown beyond the consent of the governed and promised to shrink it, while adding that his goal was not to do away with government but to make it work.
look.cite: Ronald Reagan, first inaugural address, January 20, 1981 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Compare this to Franklin Roosevelt's promise of government action in 1933. What had changed between the two crises to make each message persuasive in its moment?

check.q: What did Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign demonstrate, according to the lesson?
choices: That Illinois always ratified amendments quickly
That a grassroots movement on the right could defeat one on the left
That Congress had rejected the amendment
That the amendment passed in 1982
check.why: Her Illinois-based campaign helped stop ratification three states short, a model conservatives carried into 1980.

check.q: What did supply-side economics predict would happen after the 1981 tax cuts?
choices: Inflation would rise
Unemployment would rise permanently
Growth would be strong enough that revenue would recover
The national debt would fall to zero
check.why: The theory held that lower taxes would spur growth that made up for lost revenue; the lesson notes the debt tripled instead.

check.q: Which fact do skeptics cite against the idea of a Reagan Revolution?
choices: Reagan lost the 1984 election
Reagan raised the top tax rate
Reagan ended the Cold War alone
Social Security, Medicare and federal spending as a share of the economy barely changed
check.why: The lesson presents both sides: taxes and tone changed, but the biggest programs and overall spending did not.

lessons.title: The Cold War Ends
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1985 and 1991 the Cold War ended without a shot fired between the superpowers, through American pressure, Soviet reform and the choices of ordinary people in Eastern Europe.
reading: In 1983 the Cold War felt as dangerous as it had in 1962. Reagan called the Soviet Union an evil empire and proposed a space-based missile shield the press named Star Wars. In September a Soviet fighter shot down a Korean airliner, killing everyone aboard. That November, a NATO exercise called Able Archer was so realistic that some Soviet officers feared it was cover for a real attack. Yet the year before, about a million people had rallied in New York's Central Park for a freeze on nuclear weapons, the largest protest in American history to that point. Public fear and a new Soviet leader would change the decade's direction.

Mikhail Gorbachev took power in March 1985 and launched *glasnost*, openness, and *perestroika*, restructuring, to save a Soviet economy that could not feed itself or match American spending. He and Reagan met four times. In December 1987 they signed the *INF Treaty*, the first agreement to eliminate an entire class of nuclear missiles. Earlier that year, standing at the Berlin Wall, Reagan had challenged Gorbachev, in words this book paraphrases, to open the gate and tear down the wall. The Soviet war in Afghanistan, begun in 1979, was draining money and lives, and the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster exposed how much the system hid.

The end came from below. In June 1989 the Polish union *Solidarity* won free elections. Hungary opened its border to the West. On the night of November 9, 1989, after a confused East German announcement, crowds surged to the Berlin Wall and guards, with no orders to shoot, opened the gates. Within weeks Czechoslovakia's communist government fell peacefully. Germany reunited in October 1990. A coup by hard-liners in Moscow failed in August 1991, and on December 25, 1991, the Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin. In between, in early 1991, the United States led a coalition that drove Iraq's army out of Kuwait in a ground war of about one hundred hours, the first test of the new order.

Who ended the Cold War? One argument credits Reagan's military buildup, which the Soviets could not match. Another credits Gorbachev, who refused to send tanks as earlier leaders had in 1956 and 1968. A third credits the people in the streets of Warsaw, Leipzig and Prague. A fourth points to decades of economic failure that made collapse a matter of time. Historians weigh all four with the archives now open in Moscow. At home, the *peace dividend* had a local cost: Congress closed dozens of bases, including Chanute Air Force Base in Rantoul, Illinois, and Fort Sheridan north of Chicago, both shut in 1993.

words.d: Gorbachev's policy of openness, allowing more free speech and honest news in the Soviet Union
Gorbachev's restructuring of the Soviet economy and government after 1985
the 1987 U.S.-Soviet treaty that eliminated all intermediate-range nuclear missiles
the Polish independent trade union whose 1989 election victory began the fall of communism in Eastern Europe
money freed for other uses when military spending fell after the Cold War

look.title: Night at the Wall
look.text: November 9, 1989, near midnight, Bornholmer Street crossing, East Berlin. Thousands of people press against a gate that has been closed for twenty-eight years. The guards have a few dozen rifles and no instructions; their phone calls to headquarters go unanswered. A West Berlin crowd on the other side chants. A lieutenant colonel looks at the faces, then at his men, and orders the barrier raised.
look.prompt: The officer could have followed the old rules and waited. What made this moment different from 1956 in Hungary or 1968 in Prague, when Soviet tanks rolled?

check.q: What made the INF Treaty of 1987 a first?
choices: It eliminated an entire class of nuclear missiles rather than limiting their number
It ended the Soviet war in Afghanistan
It reunited Germany
It created NATO
check.why: Earlier treaties capped weapons; the INF Treaty removed intermediate-range missiles entirely.

check.q: Why does the lesson say the end of the Cold War came from below?
choices: Because Reagan ordered the wall opened
Because elections in Poland, open borders in Hungary and crowds at the Berlin Wall forced change before governments decided
Because Soviet tanks crushed the protests
Because the United Nations voted to end it
check.why: Ordinary people in Eastern Europe acted first, and Gorbachev chose not to send tanks.

check.q: Which evidence would best test the claim that Reagan's buildup ended the Cold War?
choices: The number of Reagan's television speeches
American election results from 1984
Soviet archives showing what its leaders thought they could afford
The height of the Berlin Wall
check.why: The claim is about Soviet decisions, so Soviet records are the evidence that could confirm or challenge it.

lessons.title: The Nineties and the Internet
lessons.mainIdea: The 1990s brought a long economic expansion, a budget surplus, bitter partisan fights and a new network, built in part in Illinois, that changed daily life.
reading: Bill Clinton won in 1992 by running on the economy while a Texas businessman, Ross Perot, took nearly a fifth of the vote as an independent. Clinton raised taxes on high earners to shrink the deficit and signed *NAFTA*, which removed most trade barriers with Canada and Mexico in 1994; unions warned it would send factories south, and supporters promised cheaper goods and new markets. In 1994 Republicans led by Newt Gingrich won the House for the first time in forty years. Two government shutdowns followed in 1995 and 1996. Clinton then signed a Republican welfare reform bill that set time limits on cash aid. By 1998 the budget was in *surplus* for the first time since 1969, and by 2000 unemployment was down to four percent. In December 1998 the House impeached Clinton for lying under oath about an affair; the Senate acquitted him.

Beneath the politics, a network was growing. The Defense Department had linked a few university computers in 1969. In 1991 a British scientist, Tim Berners-Lee, released the World Wide Web, a way to link documents across that network. It stayed a tool for scientists until 1993, when a team of students and staff at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois in Urbana released Mosaic, the first popular *browser* that showed pictures and text on the same page and worked with a mouse click. Two of its creators, Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, left to found Netscape in 1994. Amazon opened in 1995, Google in 1998. In 1995 about one American adult in seven used the internet; by 2000 it was half.

Money poured in. Companies with no profits sold shares for billions, and the NASDAQ stock index, heavy with technology firms, roughly doubled in 1999 alone. In March 2000 the *dot-com bubble* burst, and the index lost about three quarters of its value over the next two and a half years. Yet the cables and the habits stayed. Meanwhile, the decade's prosperity was uneven. Factory employment kept falling, wages for workers without college degrees barely rose, and *globalization*, the tightening links of trade and money across borders, brought cheap electronics and lost jobs to the same towns. Chicago's downtown boomed while the old mill neighborhoods on the Southeast Side did not.

How should historians read the 1990s? One view calls it a golden decade: peace, surplus, falling crime, the web. Another sees a bubble in stocks and in confidence that popped in 2000 and 2001. A third asks whose decade it was, using Congressional Budget Office data showing that the top one percent's share of income rose steadily. The internet's early promise was that anyone could publish and everyone could know; later chapters of this story test that promise. To judge, compare the 1995 and 2000 adoption numbers with what people actually did online, then and now.

words.d: the North American Free Trade Agreement of 1994 among the United States, Canada and Mexico
the condition when government collects more in a year than it spends; the opposite of a deficit
software for viewing pages on the World Wide Web; Mosaic, from Illinois, was the first popular one
the late-1990s surge in internet stock prices that collapsed starting in March 2000
the tightening links of trade, money, people and information across national borders

look.title: Americans Online
look.unit: % of U.S. adults who use the internet
look.prompt: Which five-year jump is the biggest, and what happened in those years to explain it? What does this table not tell you about how people used the internet?

check.q: What was NAFTA's central trade-off, as the lesson presents it?
choices: Higher taxes versus lower spending
War versus peace with Mexico
A budget surplus versus a deficit
Cheaper goods and new markets versus factory jobs moving abroad
check.why: Supporters promised prices and markets; unions warned of lost factories. The lesson gives both sides.

check.q: Why was Mosaic, created at the University of Illinois in 1993, important?
choices: It was the first popular browser to show pictures and text together and work by mouse click, opening the web to ordinary people
It was the first computer network
It was the first online store
It invented email
check.why: The web existed from 1991, but Mosaic made it usable for non-scientists.

check.q: Which evidence supports the view that the 1990s prosperity was uneven?
choices: The budget surplus of 1998
Congressional Budget Office data on the top one percent's rising share of income
The four percent unemployment rate
The growth of the NASDAQ in 1999
check.why: Income share data show who gained most; the other figures show overall growth, not its distribution.

lessons.title: September 11
lessons.mainIdea: On September 11, 2001, nineteen al-Qaeda hijackers killed nearly three thousand people in under two hours, and the attacks reshaped American law, war and daily life.
reading: At 8:46 on a clear Tuesday morning, American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York. At 9:03 a second plane hit the South Tower, and millions watching live understood it was no accident. At 9:37 a third plane hit the Pentagon outside Washington. On the fourth, United Flight 93, passengers who had learned by phone what was happening fought the hijackers, and the plane crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at 10:03. The South Tower fell at 9:59, the North at 10:28. Nearly three thousand people died, including 343 New York City firefighters who had climbed into the towers. The nineteen hijackers belonged to *al-Qaeda*, a network led by Osama bin Laden and sheltered by the Taliban government of Afghanistan, which had bombed two American embassies in 1998 and a Navy ship in 2000.

Every civilian plane in the country was grounded for days. In Chicago the Sears Tower was evacuated and the skies over O'Hare went silent. Blood banks had lines around the block. On September 18 Congress authorized the president to use force against those responsible; only one member voted no. President George W. Bush's approval rating rose to about ninety percent, and trust in government briefly reached levels not seen since the 1960s. At the same time, attacks on Muslims, Sikhs and Arab Americans spiked. Bush visited a Washington mosque six days after the attacks to say, in a paraphrase, that Islam was a religion of peace and that those who harassed Muslim Americans did not represent the country.

The legal changes came fast. The *Patriot Act*, signed in October 2001, expanded the government's power to conduct *surveillance*, share intelligence and track money. The *Department of Homeland Security*, created in 2002, combined twenty-two agencies, including a new one to screen airline passengers. A prison opened at the Guantanamo Bay naval base in Cuba in 2002 to hold suspects outside ordinary courts. The *9/11 Commission*, a bipartisan body, reported in 2004 that the FBI and CIA had each held pieces of the plot but had not shared them, and Congress created a Director of National Intelligence. Later revelations, in 2005 and again in 2013, showed the government had collected Americans' phone and internet records on a scale few had imagined.

For a student born after 2001, this is history, and it comes with the usual problems of evidence. The Commission's report is a federal document, public and searchable. Thousands of oral histories, from firefighters to office workers, are preserved in New York. The hardest questions are about trade-offs: how much privacy for how much safety, and who decides. Those questions did not begin on September 11, but that morning changed the answers a majority of Americans were willing to accept.

words.d: the terrorist network led by Osama bin Laden that carried out the September 11 attacks
the October 2001 law that expanded government powers to monitor communications and track money
close watching of people or communications by the government or others
the cabinet department created in 2002 to coordinate border, transportation and disaster security
the bipartisan body whose 2004 report explained the attacks and the failures that let them happen

look.title: A Chicago Classroom, Mid-Morning
look.text: A teacher wheels a television on a cart into a Chicago high school classroom around 9:15 Central time. Students watch a second tower burn. Someone's parent works in the Sears Tower, which is being emptied. By noon the school has decided to stay open; by three the sky is empty of planes for the first time any of them can remember. A student writes the date on a notebook page and nothing else.
look.prompt: That notebook page, the school's announcement and the television broadcast are all sources. What could each tell a historian, and what could none of them tell?

check.q: Why does the lesson say the passengers on Flight 93 matter to the story?
choices: They were the only victims that day
They landed the plane safely
Having learned what was happening, they fought the hijackers, and the plane went down in a field instead of a target
They were members of al-Qaeda
check.why: Phone calls told them about the other planes, and their resistance ended the fourth attack in Pennsylvania.

check.q: What did the 9/11 Commission find about the FBI and CIA?
choices: They had planned the attacks
They had never heard of al-Qaeda
They had shared everything and still failed
Each held pieces of the plot but did not share them with the other
check.why: The 2004 report blamed a failure to connect information, leading to the creation of a Director of National Intelligence.

check.q: Which of these was a direct legal result of the attacks?
choices: The Patriot Act's expansion of surveillance powers
The War Powers Resolution
The end of the Cold War
The Freedom of Information Act
check.why: The Patriot Act was signed in October 2001; the other laws came from the 1970s and 1980s.

lessons.title: The Wars That Followed
lessons.mainIdea: The United States fought in Afghanistan for twenty years and in Iraq for nearly nine, wars that cost trillions of dollars and thousands of lives and whose results are still debated.
reading: American and allied forces attacked Afghanistan on October 7, 2001. The Taliban government fell within weeks, but bin Laden escaped across the mountains into Pakistan. What began as a hunt became a twenty-year effort to build a government, train an army and fight a Taliban that never went away. Navy SEALs killed bin Laden in Pakistan on May 2, 2011. The last American troops left in August 2021, and the Taliban retook the capital before they were gone. About 2,400 American service members died in Afghanistan, along with far larger numbers of Afghans. It was the longest war in American history.

Iraq was a choice. The Bush administration argued for *preemption*: striking a threat before it struck. Officials said Iraq held *weapons of mass destruction* and had ties to al-Qaeda. Congress authorized force in October 2002; that month a state senator named Barack Obama told a Chicago rally he opposed what he called a dumb war. The invasion began March 20, 2003, and Baghdad fell in three weeks. No banned weapons were ever found; a government inspection team said so in 2004. An *insurgency* and a civil war between Sunni and Shia Iraqis followed, and photographs of American guards abusing prisoners at Abu Ghraib shocked the world. A *surge* of troops in 2007 reduced the violence. Combat forces left in December 2011; the Islamic State seized much of Iraq in 2014 and drew Americans back. About 4,500 Americans died in Iraq. Estimates of Iraqi deaths start above a hundred thousand.

At home the wars were fought by a small share of the country. There was no draft; fewer than one percent of Americans served, and National Guard units, including Illinois brigades, deployed repeatedly. Hundreds of thousands of *veterans* came home with brain injuries or post-traumatic stress, and their care will cost the government for decades. The Senate reported in 2014 that the CIA had tortured prisoners, including by waterboarding, and argued it produced little useful intelligence; defenders disputed that. Researchers who add up the spending, the borrowing and the future care estimate the post-9/11 wars will cost trillions of dollars.

How should a student judge these wars? Start with what was claimed in 2002 and 2003 and set it beside what was known then and learned later. Read the 2002 debate in Congress, where the arguments on both sides are recorded. Count the costs in lives and dollars, and ask what the alternatives were. Then notice that a law passed in three days in September 2001 has been cited for military action in many countries for more than twenty years, and ask who should decide when a war ends.

words.d: attacking a threat before it attacks you; the Bush administration's argument for the Iraq war
nuclear, chemical or biological weapons; none were found in Iraq after 2003
an armed uprising against an occupying force or government, as in Iraq after 2003
the 2007 increase of about thirty thousand American troops in Iraq
a person who has served in the armed forces

look.title: Sixty Words of Authority
look.text: In a paraphrase of the joint resolution Congress passed a week after the attacks, the president was authorized to use all necessary and appropriate force against the nations, organizations or persons he determined had planned, authorized, committed or aided the attacks of September 11, or had harbored those who did, in order to prevent future acts of terrorism against the United States.
look.cite: Authorization for Use of Military Force, September 18, 2001 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Who decides which groups are covered by this language? Why might a law this short and this broad be used for decades, and what would a narrower version look like?

check.q: What was the main stated reason for invading Iraq in 2003?
choices: Iraq had attacked the United States on September 11
The claim that Iraq held weapons of mass destruction and had ties to al-Qaeda
Iraq had invaded Afghanistan
The United Nations ordered it
check.why: The administration argued for preemption based on those claims; no banned weapons were found.

check.q: Why does the lesson say the wars were fought by a small share of the country?
choices: Because the wars were short
Because most soldiers were foreign allies
Because there was no draft and fewer than one percent of Americans served
Because Congress refused to fund them
check.why: Without a draft, repeated deployments fell on volunteers and National Guard units.

check.q: What method does the lesson recommend for judging the Iraq war?
choices: Trust the most recent news story
Ask only veterans
Count only the dollars spent
Compare what was claimed in 2002 and 2003 with what was known then and learned later
check.why: Setting claims beside evidence, and reading the recorded debate, is how historians test a decision.

lessons.title: The Crash of 2008
lessons.mainIdea: A housing bubble built on risky mortgages and complex financial bets burst in 2008, causing the worst downturn since the Depression and a fierce argument over bailouts.
reading: From 2000 to 2006 the price of an average American house roughly doubled. Lenders, confident prices would keep rising, offered *subprime mortgages* to borrowers with weak credit, often with low starting payments that jumped after two years. Banks did not keep these loans. Through *securitization* they bundled thousands of mortgages into bonds and sold them to investors around the world, and rating agencies stamped many of the bundles as safe as government debt. Other firms sold insurance on those bonds without setting money aside to pay claims. The whole structure assumed that home prices in Chicago, Phoenix and Miami could not all fall at once.

They did. Prices began sliding in 2006, payments jumped, and *foreclosure* notices spread through neighborhoods, hitting Black and Latino families, who had been steered toward the riskiest loans, hardest. In March 2008 the investment bank Bear Stearns collapsed and was sold with government help. On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in American history and no rescue came. The next day the government lent eighty-five billion dollars to the insurer AIG to keep it from failing. Credit froze: banks stopped lending even to each other. On September 29 the House voted down a rescue plan and the Dow fell 777 points in a day. Four days later Congress passed *TARP*, a seven-hundred-billion-dollar *bailout* that bought stakes in banks and later rescued General Motors and Chrysler.

The *Great Recession* officially ran from December 2007 to June 2009, but the damage lasted longer. The economy lost nearly nine million jobs, and unemployment reached ten percent in October 2009. Millions of families lost homes. In February 2009 Congress passed a stimulus of about eight hundred billion dollars in spending and tax cuts, and the Federal Reserve held interest rates near zero for seven years. Anger ran in two directions. On February 19, 2009, a television reporter on the floor of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange denounced help for struggling borrowers, a rant credited with sparking the Tea Party movement. In 2011 Occupy Wall Street protested the rescue of banks whose executives were never prosecuted. Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010 to tighten rules on lenders.

Whose fault was it? The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, a federal body, concluded in 2011 that the crisis was avoidable and blamed regulators, lenders and the rating agencies; dissenting members blamed government housing policy and a global glut of savings. Was the bailout right? Defenders say it prevented a second Great Depression at a profit to taxpayers; critics say it saved the people who caused the crisis while homeowners got little. To weigh these, compare the response of 1929 to 1933 with the response of 2008, and follow the unemployment numbers year by year.

words.d: a home loan to a borrower with weak credit, often with payments that rise sharply after a few years
bundling loans into bonds that can be sold to investors
a lender taking back a home when the borrower cannot pay the mortgage
the Troubled Asset Relief Program, the seven-hundred-billion-dollar rescue of banks and automakers passed in October 2008
government money used to keep a failing company or bank from collapsing
the downturn from December 2007 to June 2009, the deepest since the 1930s

look.title: Unemployment Before and After the Crash
look.unit: % of the labor force, annual average
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, annual averages
look.prompt: The recession officially ended in June 2009, yet the rate was higher in 2010. How long did it take to get back to 2007 levels, and what does that say about how recessions are measured?

check.q: Why did a fall in house prices threaten banks around the world?
choices: Mortgages had been bundled into bonds and sold globally, so losses spread to whoever held them
Foreign banks owned most American homes
The government had guaranteed every mortgage
House prices had never fallen before
check.why: Securitization spread the risk of subprime loans far beyond the original lenders.

check.q: What happened on September 15, 2008?
choices: Congress passed TARP
Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in American history with no rescue
The Dow fell 777 points
The recession officially ended
check.why: Lehman's collapse froze credit; the Dow's fall came September 29 and TARP passed October 3.

check.q: What did the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission's majority conclude?
choices: That the crisis was caused only by borrowers
That nothing could have prevented it
That the crisis was avoidable and regulators, lenders and rating agencies were to blame
That the bailout caused the crisis
check.why: The 2011 report called it avoidable; dissenters pointed instead to housing policy and global savings.

lessons.title: A President from Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Barack Obama rose through Chicago organizing and Illinois politics to become the first Black president, and his eight years show how a presidency is shaped by crisis and opposition.
reading: Barack Obama was born in Honolulu in 1961 to a mother from Kansas and a father from Kenya. In 1985 he took a job as a *community organizer* on Chicago's Far South Side, working with churches in Roseland and the Altgeld Gardens housing project in neighborhoods left behind when Wisconsin Steel closed. He went to Harvard Law School, became the first Black president of its law review, and returned to Chicago to practice civil rights law, teach at the University of Chicago and marry Michelle Robinson, who grew up in South Shore. He won a state senate seat from Hyde Park in 1996, lost a 2000 race for Congress, and in 2004 gave a convention speech that made him famous. Illinois elected him to the U.S. Senate that fall. Others had cleared the ground: Harold Washington became Chicago's first Black mayor in 1983, and Carol Moseley Braun of Illinois the first Black woman senator in 1992.

He announced for president in Springfield on February 10, 2007, ran against Hillary Clinton in a long primary that began with a win in Iowa, and faced John McCain in the fall. The financial crash in September 2008 turned the race toward the economy. Obama won about fifty-three percent of the vote and 365 electoral votes, with record turnout among young and Black voters, and celebrated in Grant Park. Twelve weeks later he took office with the economy losing hundreds of thousands of jobs a month.

His first two years produced the *stimulus*, the auto rescue, the Dodd-Frank financial rules and, in March 2010, the *Affordable Care Act*, which required most Americans to carry health insurance, expanded Medicaid and barred insurers from refusing people with existing conditions; by 2016 about twenty million more people had coverage. Every Republican in Congress voted against it. In the 2010 *midterm election* Democrats lost sixty-three House seats, and the rest of the presidency was a struggle with a divided Congress over budgets and debt. Abroad, Obama ended combat in Iraq, expanded drone strikes, ordered the raid that killed bin Laden and signed a climate agreement in Paris in 2015. He won re-election over Mitt Romney in 2012. In 2015 the Supreme Court recognized same-sex marriage nationwide. In 2016 the Senate refused for nearly a year to consider his Supreme Court nominee.

Judging a presidency this recent is hard, and historians know it. Supporters point to the recovery, the health law and the symbolism of the first Black president; critics on the right cite debt and regulation, and critics on the left cite deportations, drone strikes and unprosecuted bankers. Under the *Presidential Records Act*, his papers belong to the public and are opening in stages; the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park, a few miles from where he organized, will house exhibits while the records themselves are digital. The ranking will change as the files open, as it did for Truman and Reagan.

words.d: a person who helps neighborhood residents build power to win changes from officials and businesses
government spending and tax cuts meant to boost a weak economy, such as the 2009 recovery act
the 2010 health law that expanded coverage through insurance rules, subsidies and Medicaid
the congressional election held two years into a president's term, which the president's party usually loses seats in
the 1978 law making a president's official records public property, opened in stages after the term ends

look.title: The Speech in the Park
look.text: In a paraphrase of his remarks that night, Obama said that anyone who still doubted that America was a place where all things were possible, or still questioned the power of democracy, had received their answer. He described Ann Nixon Cooper, a one-hundred-six-year-old voter in Atlanta born when women and Black Americans could not vote, and listed what she had lived to see: the Depression, the war, the buses of Montgomery, a man on the moon. He asked what change his own daughters might see if they lived as long.
look.cite: Barack Obama, election night remarks, Grant Park, Chicago, November 4, 2008 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why build a speech around one voter's lifetime rather than around policy? What does that choice tell you about how the speaker wanted the night to be remembered?

check.q: Where did Obama work as a community organizer, and why does the lesson mention Wisconsin Steel?
choices: In Springfield, because the mill was there
In Hyde Park, because the university owned the mill
In Washington, because Congress regulated steel
In Roseland and Altgeld Gardens, neighborhoods left behind when the mill closed in 1980
check.why: The lesson connects his organizing to the deindustrialization described earlier in the chapter.

check.q: What did the Affordable Care Act do?
choices: Required most people to carry insurance, expanded Medicaid and barred refusals for existing conditions
Created Medicare
Made health care free for everyone
Ended private insurance
check.why: The 2010 law worked through insurance rules and Medicaid expansion; about twenty million more people gained coverage by 2016.

check.q: Why does the lesson say the ranking of Obama's presidency will change?
choices: Because he will run again
Because presidential records open in stages and historians revise judgments as files become available
Because the Supreme Court will rule on it
Because Congress votes on rankings
check.why: Under the Presidential Records Act, papers open over time, and assessments of Truman and Reagan changed the same way.

lessons.title: Polarization, Screens and a Pandemic
lessons.mainIdea: Since about 2010 American politics has grown more polarized, social media has changed how people learn and argue, and the COVID-19 pandemic tested government and trust at the same time.
reading: *Polarization* means the two parties moving apart. The evidence is in the numbers. In 1994 about one voter in five held a very unfavorable view of the other party; by 2022 more than half did. Votes in Congress fall along party lines far more often than in the 1970s. Explanations compete: the sorting of conservatives into one party and liberals into the other, primaries that reward the loudest candidates, safe districts, and cable news. In 2016 Donald Trump won the presidency in the Electoral College while losing the popular vote. In 2020 Joe Biden defeated him; Trump's claims of a stolen election lost in more than sixty court cases, and on January 6, 2021, a crowd of his supporters stormed the Capitol to stop the count. The House impeached Trump twice; the Senate acquitted him both times. In 2024 he won a second, non-consecutive term.

The screens changed in the middle of this. Facebook opened to the public in 2006, the iPhone arrived in 2007, and within a decade most Americans carried a feed in their pocket. Platforms make money from attention, so an *algorithm* chooses what each person sees, favoring posts that get a reaction. Researchers disagree about how much this drives polarization; some studies find feeds mostly confirm what people already think, others find real effects on anger and *misinformation*. A Senate committee found that a Russian agency ran fake American accounts during the 2016 campaign. Doctors debate the effect on teenagers' mental health. What is not in dispute is that the way most people first learn about an event changed more between 2005 and 2015 than in the previous fifty years.

Then a virus arrived. The second known American case of COVID-19 was a Chicago woman, confirmed in January 2020. On March 11 the World Health Organization declared a *pandemic*; on March 21 Illinois ordered residents to stay home, and schools went online. Unemployment hit nearly fifteen percent in April 2020, the highest since the Depression, and Congress passed a rescue package of about two trillion dollars. On May 25 a Minneapolis police officer killed George Floyd, and protests filled cities including Chicago. Vaccines, developed in under a year, were authorized in December 2020. By 2023 more than a million Americans had died, with deaths falling unevenly by age, race, income and region. Masks and vaccines became partisan markers, and students lost months of learning. Trust in institutions, already low, fell further for many.

These are events you or your family lived through, which makes them hard to see as history. Claims about them contradict one another, and some of the people who made those claims are still making them. One tool is the count of *excess deaths*, the number of people who died beyond what would be expected in a normal year, which cuts through arguments about labels on death certificates. Another is to ask what a historian in 2075 would need: the emails, the school board recordings, the texts between friends, the memory of the empty expressway. Most of that will vanish unless someone saves it.

words.d: the movement of political parties and their supporters toward opposite poles, with less overlap between them
the set of rules a platform uses to decide which posts each person sees
false or misleading information, whether or not it is spread on purpose
an outbreak of disease across many countries at once; COVID-19 was declared one in March 2020
deaths above the number expected in a normal year, a way to measure a disaster's toll

look.title: Two Phones, One Night
look.text: Two cousins in the same Chicago apartment scroll their phones on the evening of a big news event in 2020. One feed shows a video clip with a furious caption, shared forty thousand times. The other shows the same clip cut ten seconds later, with a calm explanation, shared four hundred times. Neither cousin has seen the full video. By morning each is certain the other has been fooled.
look.prompt: What would each cousin need to do to find out what actually happened, and why is that harder than it was when both would have watched the same ten o'clock news?

check.q: What evidence does the lesson give that polarization has increased?
choices: More people vote than in the 1970s
There are more television channels
The share of voters with a very unfavorable view of the other party rose from about one in five to more than half
The parties changed their names
check.why: The lesson cites the 1994 to 2022 shift in how partisans view each other, along with party-line votes in Congress.

check.q: Why do social media feeds tend to favor posts that provoke a reaction?
choices: Because the government requires it
Because users request it
Because such posts are more accurate
Because platforms earn money from attention, and algorithms select for what keeps people engaged
check.why: The lesson explains the business model behind the algorithm, while noting researchers disagree about its effects.

check.q: Why does the lesson recommend counting excess deaths?
choices: It cuts through arguments about how individual deaths were labeled
It counts only deaths in hospitals
It was invented for COVID-19
It ignores older people
check.why: Comparing total deaths to a normal year measures a disaster's toll without depending on contested death certificates.

lessons.title: Writing History While It Happens
lessons.mainIdea: The recent past is the hardest history to write because the sources are incomplete, the outcomes unknown and the historian is a participant, so historians use rules to keep themselves honest.
reading: Harry Truman left office in 1953 with one of the lowest approval ratings ever recorded; historians now rank him among the better presidents. Reagan was dismissed by many scholars in 1989 and reassessed after his diaries and letters were published. Distance changes the view, and so do the records. Under the Presidential Records Act, a president's papers go to the National Archives and open in stages, with the most sensitive files closed for twelve years or more, and classified documents reviewed after twenty-five. Since the 1990s most of those records are *born-digital*: emails, texts, drafts saved over drafts. A tweet can be deleted; a web page can change. The Internet Archive has saved copies of pages since 1996, but only some of them.

Historians working close to the present follow rules. Source every claim: who said it, when, and what did they want. *Corroborate*: find a second, independent record before believing the first. Separate journalism, the first draft, from history, which waits for the drafts underneath. Watch for *hindsight*, the trap of judging a 2003 decision by what was learned in 2004. Watch for *presentism*, judging the past by today's values without first understanding its own. And count the silent: the warehouse worker in 2020 who left no essay, the family in 1980 whose mill closed, the grandmother who watched Watergate on a black-and-white set. Oral history projects, including ones at Chicago museums and libraries, exist to record them before they are gone.

The chapter's own events show how interpretations move. In 1974 Watergate seemed to prove the system worked; a year later the Church Committee showed how much of the system had failed unseen. In 2008 the crash was blamed on greedy borrowers, then on greedy banks, then, by a federal commission, on regulators who looked away; the arguments continue with better data. In 2020 the pandemic's toll was fought over daily; the excess-death counts settled some of it, and more will be settled when hospital and government records open. None of these stories is finished. Each got clearer as evidence arrived and as the people writing it were no longer the people living it.

That makes you a *primary source*. What you keep from this year, a screenshot, a diary, a recording of a grandparent describing a gas line in 1979 or a classroom on September 11, 2001, or an empty street in March 2020, is what a historian will have. The next chapter of this course asks you to choose a question about your own place and pursue it through evidence. This chapter's lesson is the starting rule: the recent past is not yet history, but it is already evidence, and someone has to save it.

words.d: records created on computers, such as emails and texts, with no paper original
to confirm a claim with a second, independent source
judging a past decision by outcomes that were unknown when it was made
judging the past by present-day values without first understanding its own
a record created at the time by a participant or witness

look.title: A Box in the Closet
look.text: A family in Chicago's Pullman neighborhood cleans out a closet and finds a box. Inside: a 1974 odd-even gas rationing card, a union pay stub from Wisconsin Steel dated February 1980, a newspaper from September 12, 2001, a foreclosure notice from 2009 with a handwritten note on the back, a homemade cloth mask, and a phone that no longer turns on. Nothing is labeled.
look.prompt: Which items can a historian read without help, which need a living person to explain, and which will be gone in fifty years unless someone acts now?

check.q: Why did the assessment of Truman and Reagan change over time?
choices: Because they were re-elected later
Because distance from events and newly opened records changed what historians could see
Because Congress passed a law ranking presidents
Because their approval ratings were secret
check.why: The lesson uses both as examples of how records and time move interpretations.

check.q: What is hindsight, as the lesson defines it?
choices: Remembering the past accurately
Judging the past by today's values
Judging a past decision by outcomes that were unknown when it was made
Reading only primary sources
check.why: The lesson warns against judging 2003 by what was learned in 2004; presentism is the values trap, a different error.

check.q: Why does the lesson call the student a primary source?
choices: Because students write the textbooks
Because students are always right about the present
Because teachers cite students
Because what a witness keeps from this year becomes the record a future historian will use
check.why: A screenshot, a diary or a recorded interview made now is a record created at the time by a witness.

review.q: Which sequence correctly orders the Watergate events?

Resignation, break-in, hearings, Supreme Court ruling
Supreme Court ruling, break-in, pardon, hearings
Saturday Night Massacre, break-in, resignation, hearings

review.q: How did the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks connect to the recession of 1981 and 1982?
choices: They caused the Federal Reserve to lower rates, which caused a recession
They fed inflation that the Federal Reserve then crushed with very high interest rates, producing the recession
They had no connection; the recession was caused by NAFTA
They ended inflation on their own
review.why: Volcker's Fed raised rates above twenty percent to stop the inflation the oil shocks had fueled, and unemployment neared eleven percent.

choices: Reagan won forty-nine states in 1984
The top income tax rate fell to twenty-eight percent
Federal spending as a share of the economy and the largest programs barely changed
The national debt tripled

review.q: Which event in this chapter came first?
choices: The Berlin Wall opened
Mosaic was released in Urbana
Lehman Brothers collapsed
The INF Treaty was signed
review.why: The INF Treaty was December 1987; the Wall opened November 1989; Mosaic came in 1993; Lehman fell in 2008.

review.q: Compare the government's response to September 11 with its response to Watergate. What is the main difference the chapter shows?
choices: After Watergate Congress limited presidential power; after September 11 Congress expanded it
Both events led to a president resigning
Both events lowered public trust in government
After September 11 Congress abolished the CIA
review.why: The 1970s produced the War Powers Resolution and oversight; 2001 produced the AUMF, the Patriot Act and Homeland Security, and trust briefly rose.

review.q: What links Wisconsin Steel, Barack Obama and the 2008 crash in this chapter?
choices: Obama worked at the mill before it closed
The mill's 1980 closing shaped the neighborhoods where Obama organized, and the same South Side areas were hit hard by 2008 foreclosures
The mill caused the 2008 crash
The mill reopened under the stimulus
review.why: The chapter traces deindustrialization, organizing and foreclosure through the same part of Chicago.

review.q: A historian in 2075 wants to study the 2020 pandemic in Chicago. Which source problem does the chapter predict?
choices: Too few people wrote about it
Every record was on paper and will survive
Born-digital records such as texts and posts can be deleted or lost unless someone saves them
The government has already published a complete history
review.why: The chapter stresses that digital records vanish and that witnesses must preserve them.

review.q: Why does the chapter warn against hindsight when judging the decision to invade Iraq?
choices: Because the decision was obviously correct
Because no one knew Iraq existed in 2003
Because historians should never judge wars
Because the lack of weapons was learned in 2004, and fair judgment starts with what was known and argued in 2002 and 2003
review.why: The method is to set the claims of the time beside the evidence then available, then add what was learned later.
